curriculum.lesson_evidence: Context and setting of a novel include time, place, social conditions and how the narrative world pressures characters. Readers distinguish textual setting details from unsupported guesses about the author’s whole life.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 4 NESA English alignment using catalogue outcome codes (EN4-*); content-point mapping and independent NESA verification remain pending.

lesson.child_mission: Context and setting of a novel include time, place, social conditions and how the narrative world pressures characters. Readers distinguish textual setting details from unsupported guesses about the author’s whole life.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same strategy to an unfamiliar topic or audience, then compare the effect of two different choices.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Collect five setting details and write two inferences about pressure on a character, labelled inference vs detail.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: details textual; inferences cautious; labels correct.

CHECK
Confusing setting summary with theme announcement without evidence.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Independently produce a setting dossier page (map/list + pressures) for the class novel with cited page/chapter references as available.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Context and setting of a novel include time, place, social conditions and how the narrative world pressures characters. Readers distinguish textual setting details from unsupported guesses about the author’s whole life.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

teach_steps.explain:
Context and setting of a novel include time, place, social conditions and how the narrative world pressures characters. Readers distinguish textual setting details from unsupported guesses about the author’s whole life.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
